name: neurofunk-reese-machine
idea: Cold, clinical neurofunk at 174 BPM: the lead 'performer' is a snarling, heavily processed Reese bass that mutates every bar over a tight, dry two-step drum pattern. It should sound like machinery in a fluorescent basement, with hard and metallic textures and no melody to speak of. Ask for it in a terse genre-tag style box (neurofunk, techstep, Reese bass, 174 BPM, instrumental, no intro, starts on the drop) with a strong exclude list against vocals, chops and MCs. The lyrics box opens straight on [Drop] after [Instrumental], so the first downbeat is full weight, and it stays one relentless loopable section with no breakdown.

name: jump-up-cartoon-wobble
idea: Play it for the joke. Bouncy, cartoonish jump-up DnB where a big wobbling, honking 'hoover' bass lurches around like a toddler's tantrum, over a punchy snare that cracks on every 2 and 4. The tone is gleeful vandalism, the rave equivalent of paper being thrown in the air, and the direct comic opposite of the bored school hymn before it. Ask for the music descriptively, as a scene: a rave erupts in a council basement, the bass bounces and barks from the first beat, wall-to-wall energy, instrumental only. Keep it one repeating 8-bar riff so the editor can loop it.

name: amen-jungle-pirate-tape
idea: The drummer is the star. A 1994 UK jungle track built on a frantically chopped, time-stretched Amen break with a rolling sub bass and one stabbing rave chord, recorded off a pirate radio tape so it is slightly crunchy, saturated and lo-fi. The rough, homemade, British, working-class rave sound gives the gang a native soundtrack, not a slick festival drop. Ask for it by era and production detail: 1990s jungle, hardcore breakbeat, cassette hiss, pirate radio, 165 BPM, breaks from bar one, no MC, no ragga vocal samples. The lyrics box holds only [Instrumental] and a [Break] cue at the top, so the chopped drums lead in immediately.

name: live-band-rock-dnb
idea: Human performers, not a computer. A live session drummer hammering a real kit at drum and bass tempo (175 BPM), with a punk bassist playing a fuzz-distorted bass guitar riff and a noise guitar slamming one power chord on the downbeats. It should sound like a band kicking a door in, with a raw room sound, cymbals smashing and amps feeding back, so the chaos feels physical and the tearing of paper has a matching texture. Ask for it as a band in a room: who plays what, how hard, mic'd live, instrumental, the full band crashing in together on beat one. Exclude vocals, shouting and crowd chants so nobody sings.
